newsitem.title: KENYA: FOCUS-Kenya in plea to investors, shilling weak.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Kenya in plea to investors, shilling weak.

text.p: Kenya's central bank governor Micah Cheserem, alarmed by a rapid outflow of dollars fuelled by a row with the International Monetary Fund, on Friday begged foreign investors not to abandon east Africa's economic engine.
But it was not immediately clear whether Kenya's nervous market, which has seen its shilling currency depreciate by 17 percent in two weeks, would heed the governor's latest plea.

Cheserem spoke a day after investors pulled out of Kenya's usually lucrative weekly auction of high-yield treasury bills citing market uncertainty. The row with the IMF has hurt the shilling and jolted investors.
The Fund put Kenya's aid package of up to $205 million under its Enhanced Structual Adjustment Facility in cold storage on July 31, citing concerns on graft and governance.

The World Bank swiftly followed suit and said it would delay its own disbursements of up to $71.6 million until the embattled government of President Daniel arap Moi addressed issues raised by the IMF.

"Despite the current challenges, Kenya is still an attractive location for investment. It will become even more attractive once the current outstanding economic challenges are resolved," Cheserem told a news conference.
"Kenya is still an attractive location considering the attractive interest rate it is paying. Our appeal is for investors to be patient as we resolve the current issues with the IMF," he said.

Cheserem's appeal was sparked by a dismal performance of usually lucrative treasury bills on Thursday after foreign investors pulled out in hordes. The bank only managed to auction 50 percent of the 14 billion shilling ($200 million) worth of bills offered.

"The shortfall is attributed to foreign investors who have decided to liquidate their investments citing the uncertainty arising from the recent lapse of the financial arrangement with the IMF," the bank said.
"The latest results of the treasury bill auction indicate that some foreign investors have decided to liquidate their investments and repatriate the proceeds," Cheserem said on Friday.
The shilling remained weak on Friday after marginal gains to close at 69.75 from 69.97.

Cheserem has refused to intervene to boost the shilling, saying he would leave the currency to defend itself in the market but analysts said they feared he was deliberately allowing the shilling to nosedive.
"It's not clear whether he wants the shilling to slide in favour of tourism and exporters. Maybe he has done this intentionally not just because of the IMF," said a leading dealer.
A bourse floor trader told Reuters that although Cheserem's statement might reassure anxious investors, he did not expect to see a resumption of share orders soon.
In his statement, Cheserem also appealed to exporters to bring in their export proceeds promptly.
"Avoid holding it overseas in the expectation that the shilling may depreciate further," he said.
The governor gave importers the same message: "Importers should not delay payment in the hope that the shilling may appreciate in the coming weeks."
Added to market chaos is a rising political temperature in Kenya where opposition-backed activists are pressing Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years, for sweeping constitutional reforms.

The call for reforms has degenerated into violence and up to four people were killed last Friday, including two policemen, during rallies called to support a national strike called by the opposition. ($ = 69 Kenyan Shillings)
